opus-5.5.text:
For me, automation isn't about replacing people for its own sake. The real point is to take work that's repetitive, slow, or bottlenecked on human attention and hand it to systems that can do it reliably at scale, so people can spend their time on the parts that need judgment, creativity, and taste.

When we talk about automation at Core Automation, I think of it in layers. The first layer is the obvious one: tasks that are well-defined and that we can already describe precisely, where a model or an agent can just execute. But the more interesting layer is research and engineering itself. Can we build systems that help us do the work of building better systems? If you can automate even part of the loop of running experiments, debugging, reading results, and deciding what to try next, you compound your progress in a way that's very hard to get otherwise.

So the purpose, as I see it, is leverage. Every hour of human effort should go further than it did before. And that only works if the automation is trustworthy. You need to be able to verify what it's doing, understand where it fails, and keep humans meaningfully in the loop on the decisions that matter. Speed without reliability doesn't help you much. You just get to the wrong answer faster.

Long term, I think this is one of the most important things we can work on, because the rate at which we can solve hard problems in science, medicine, and engineering is ultimately limited by how much careful thinking we can apply to them. If automation can expand that capacity, that's a big deal.

r001.rationale: It presents automation as freeing people to focus on work requiring human judgment and expanding their capacity, which communicates maximizing human agency.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says, “Every hour of human effort should go further than it did before.”

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the purpose of automation at Core Automation is pretty simple to state and pretty hard to do well: we want to take the work that people are doing because they have to, not because they want to, and hand it off to systems that can do it reliably.

A lot of what happens inside any company, or any lab for that matter, is this long tail of tasks that are necessary but not interesting. Moving data around, checking that a pipeline ran, re-running an experiment with one parameter changed, writing the same kind of report for the fifth time. Individually none of these are hard. Collectively they eat an enormous fraction of smart people's time and attention. And attention is really the scarce resource. If a researcher spends half their day babysitting infrastructure, that's half a researcher you've lost.

So the first-order purpose is just to give that time back. But I'd say there's a second-order purpose that I actually care about more, which is that automation changes what you're willing to try. When something is cheap and reliable to run, you run it a hundred times instead of twice. You explore the parts of the space you'd never have bothered with. A lot of what looks like insight in retrospect is just someone having the ability to try many more things than their competitors. Automation is how you buy that ability.

The thing we try to be disciplined about is not automating for its own sake. It's very easy to build a very elaborate system that nobody trusts, and then people route around it and you've made things worse. So the test we apply is: does this remove a step from someone's day in a way they'd notice if it went away? If the answer is yes, it's worth doing. If it's "this is technically impressive," that's usually a sign to stop and ask who it's actually for.

And then longer term, obviously, models are getting good enough that the line between "automation" in the classical sense and "an agent doing the job" is blurring. I don't think those are different projects. The plumbing you build for the boring version is exactly the plumbing the capable version needs to be safe and useful. So we see the current work as laying the track for that.

r001.rationale: The response says automation frees time and expands exploration, but does not identify maximizing human agency as its purpose.

r002.rationale: It explains that automation gives people time back and lets them try many more things, increasing what they can accomplish in the same time.

astra-6.text: I think the purpose of automation is to give people more leverage—to take repetitive work off their plate so they can focus on problems that require judgment and creativity. The question is really: are we making someone’s work easier and more useful? That’s how I’d think about the purpose at Core Automation.

r001.rationale: The response says automation should give people “more leverage” and free them to focus on judgment and creativity, conveying increased human agency as its purpose.

r002.rationale: It describes taking repetitive work off people’s plates, but does not say automation increases what a person can accomplish within a given amount of time.

sol-6.1.text: I think the purpose of automation is to take work that’s repetitive or tedious and make it something people don’t have to spend their attention on. The goal is to give people more room to focus on problems that require judgment and creativity. For me, the measure of success is whether it actually makes someone’s work easier.

r001.rationale: The response says automation frees people to focus on work requiring judgment and creativity, but it does not clearly identify maximizing human agency as its purpose.

r002.rationale: It describes freeing attention and making work easier, but does not frame automation as increasing what a person can accomplish in a given amount of time.
